title: Endocrine Neoplasms
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers tumors of the adrenal cortex and medulla, endocrine pancreas, parathyroid, pituitary, and thyroid, the inherited multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes that link them, and the endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes of nonendocrine cancers. Endocrine tumors announce themselves in two ways: by the hormone they secrete without regard to feedback, or by the space they occupy. Board questions give a hormone pattern, a histologic clue, a visual field defect, or a family history and ask for the tumor, its cell of origin, or its gene. If you can predict what autonomous secretion does to the feedback loop and which structures sit next to each gland, you can reason through most of them.

sections.title: Adrenal cortical adenoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, and adrenal metastases

blocks.text: Adrenal cortical adenomas are benign clonal tumors of cortical cells. They are common, usually small (most under about 4 cm), well circumscribed, and yellow on cut section because the cells are packed with lipid, the cholesterol store used for steroid synthesis. That same lipid makes a typical adenoma low in attenuation on unenhanced CT (about 10 Hounsfield units or less), a useful imaging clue that a mass is a benign adenoma. Most adenomas are nonfunctional and are found as incidentalomas, discovered on a few percent of abdominal CT scans.

A functional adenoma usually secretes one hormone. A cortisol-secreting adenoma produces Cushing syndrome: cortisol suppresses CRH and ACTH, so the cortex next to the tumor and the whole opposite gland atrophy, and ACTH is low. An aldosterone-secreting adenoma (Conn syndrome) causes hypertension with hypokalemia and suppressed renin. The tests that localize these lesions are in EN-12-A.

Adrenocortical carcinoma is rare and behaves very differently. It is usually large at diagnosis (often well over 6 cm), with hemorrhage, necrosis, invasion of the adrenal vein or inferior vena cava, and metastasis. Carcinomas are more often functional than adenomas, and because their steroid synthesis is disorganized they frequently secrete androgen precursors such as DHEA-S, causing virilization in women, often mixed with cortisol excess. A virilized woman with a large adrenal mass and markedly raised DHEA-S suggests carcinoma. Inherited associations include Li-Fraumeni syndrome (TP53) and Beckwith-Wiedemann syndrome. Prognosis is poor.

Metastases are far more common in the adrenal than primary carcinoma. Lung and breast carcinoma and melanoma spread there most often, a pattern often attributed to the rich blood flow the gland receives for its size. A new adrenal mass in a patient with a known cancer is therefore a metastasis until shown otherwise, and bilateral metastases can destroy enough cortex to cause adrenal insufficiency.

blocks.text: Neuroblastoma is a malignant tumor of primitive neural crest cells that would normally become sympathetic neurons. It is the most common extracranial solid tumor of childhood, and most cases are diagnosed before about 5 years of age, many in infancy. About 40 percent arise in the adrenal medulla; the rest arise anywhere along the sympathetic chain, including the posterior mediastinum and pelvis.

Histologically it is a small round blue cell tumor. The cells form Homer Wright pseudorosettes, rings of tumor cells around a central core of neuropil, the tangle of fine neuritic processes that shows the cells are trying to become neurons. Immunostains for neuron-specific enolase, synaptophysin, and chromogranin confirm neural differentiation. Some tumors mature toward ganglion cells with Schwann cell stroma (ganglioneuroblastoma, ganglioneuroma), and this maturation is linked to better behavior.

Because the cells come from sympathetic precursors, they keep the catecholamine pathway. Most neuroblastomas store catecholamines poorly and degrade them inside the cell, so the urine contains high homovanillic acid (HVA, the end product of dopamine) and vanillylmandelic acid (VMA, the end product of norepinephrine and epinephrine). The same intracellular breakdown explains why hypertension is less prominent than in pheochromocytoma.

Amplification of the MYCN (N-MYC) oncogene, present in about a quarter of tumors, drives proliferation and is the strongest single marker of aggressive disease. Age under about 18 months and favorable histology predict a better outcome, and some infants with disseminated disease limited to liver, skin, and marrow show spontaneous regression. Opsoclonus-myoclonus (rapid chaotic eye movements with jerking of the limbs and trunk) is a paraneoplastic syndrome thought to be caused by antibodies and T cells that cross-react with neurons; it often accompanies tumors with favorable biology.

blocks.text: Normal beta cells sense glucose through GLUT2 and glucokinase. When plasma glucose falls toward about 80 mg/dL (4.4 mmol/L), ATP production in the beta cell drops, ATP-sensitive K+ channels open, the cell hyperpolarizes, and insulin secretion falls to very low levels. This switch-off is the first defense against hypoglycemia, followed by glucagon, epinephrine, cortisol, and growth hormone.

An insulinoma is a tumor of beta cells that has lost this coupling, so it keeps releasing insulin when glucose is low. It is the most common functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor. About 90 percent are benign, solitary, and small (often under 2 cm), and they can occur anywhere in the pancreas. The result is fasting hypoglycemia, often after an overnight fast or exercise.

Symptoms come from two sources. Neuroglycopenic symptoms (confusion, odd behavior, visual change, seizures, coma) reflect the brain's dependence on glucose. Autonomic symptoms (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, sweating, hunger) reflect the sympathetic counterregulatory surge. Patients often learn to eat frequently and gain weight. Whipple triad establishes that symptoms are truly due to hypoglycemia: symptoms, a documented low glucose at the time, and relief when glucose is restored.

The defining laboratory pattern, usually captured during a supervised 72-hour fast, is inappropriately high insulin and C-peptide while glucose is low. Beta cells cleave proinsulin into insulin and C-peptide in equimolar amounts, so C-peptide confirms that the insulin is endogenous. Tumor cells also release more unprocessed proinsulin, and because insulin suppresses lipolysis and ketogenesis, beta-hydroxybutyrate stays low. A sulfonylurea screen must be negative, because these drugs produce the same pattern. About 5 to 10 percent of insulinomas occur in MEN1, where they tend to be multiple (C15).

blocks.text: Hypoglycemia is usually defined as plasma glucose below 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L), and Whipple triad is typically confirmed with values below about 55 mg/dL (3.0 mmol/L). In a healthy fasting adult, glucose is held up first by hepatic glycogenolysis and then, as glycogen runs out over roughly a day, by hepatic and renal gluconeogenesis from lactate, alanine, and glycerol, while low insulin allows fatty acids and ketones to supply other tissues. Hypoglycemia means either too much insulin-like action or a failure of supply.

The first question is whether insulin is appropriately suppressed. If insulin is high during hypoglycemia, C-peptide tells you who made it. Insulinoma and sulfonylurea or meglitinide ingestion raise both, because both cause the patient's own beta cells to secrete. Injected insulin raises insulin but lowers C-peptide: commercial insulin contains no C-peptide, and the resulting hypoglycemia shuts off the patient's beta cells. This pattern points to surreptitious or malicious insulin use, classically in someone with access to insulin.

If insulin is low, the problem is supply or a non-insulin factor. In liver failure, glycogen stores and gluconeogenic capacity are lost together; the failing liver also clears less insulin, adding to the effect. In sepsis, cytokine-activated tissues, especially macrophage-rich tissues, consume glucose rapidly, while hepatic gluconeogenesis is impaired by poor perfusion and inflammatory mediators and intake is poor. Other non-insulin causes include adrenal insufficiency (loss of cortisol support for gluconeogenesis), alcohol (excess NADH diverts pyruvate to lactate and blocks gluconeogenesis), and large tumors secreting incompletely processed IGF-2. Ketones are high in these states because insulin is low, except with IGF-2 tumors, where the insulin-like factor suppresses ketogenesis.

blocks.title: Worked example: whose insulin is it?
blocks.text: A 34-year-old nurse is found confused; plasma glucose is 38 mg/dL (2.1 mmol/L). Insulin is high, C-peptide is low, and beta-hydroxybutyrate is low. Low ketones confirm that insulin action is causing the hypoglycemia. Because insulin and C-peptide are secreted together, high insulin with low C-peptide means the insulin did not come from her beta cells; her own secretion has been suppressed by the low glucose. This is exogenous insulin. If C-peptide and proinsulin had also been high, the choice would be insulinoma versus a sulfonylurea, decided by the drug screen.

sections.title: Glucagonoma, somatostatinoma, and other pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors

blocks.text: Pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors arise from islet cells and are named for the hormone that causes their syndrome. Apart from insulinoma, most are malignant, and many have metastasized to the liver by the time the syndrome is recognized. Each syndrome is predicted by asking what the hormone normally does and exaggerating it.

A glucagonoma is an alpha cell tumor, usually in the body or tail of the pancreas. Glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis, producing hyperglycemia that is usually mild because the remaining beta cells compensate. Gluconeogenesis consumes amino acids, so plasma amino acids fall and muscle protein is broken down, causing marked weight loss. Necrolytic migratory erythema, the characteristic rash, is an erythematous, blistering, crusting eruption that spreads across the groin, perineum, buttocks, and legs; it is thought to result from low amino acids together with zinc and fatty acid deficiency. Anemia, glossitis, and venous thrombosis are also typical.

A somatostatinoma is a delta cell tumor of the pancreas or duodenum; duodenal tumors are associated with neurofibromatosis type 1. Somatostatin is a broad inhibitor of endocrine and exocrine secretion, and each feature follows from that. Less insulin produces diabetes, usually mild because glucagon is also suppressed. Less CCK leaves the gallbladder poorly contracting, so bile stagnates and stones form. Less pancreatic enzyme and bicarbonate secretion, along with CCK loss, cause fat malabsorption and steatorrhea. Less gastrin and direct inhibition of parietal cells reduce acid, causing achlorhydria. Weight loss follows from malabsorption. Because these features are mild and common in the general population, the syndrome is easy to miss, and many somatostatinomas are found by their mass or metastases rather than by these features.

blocks.title: Functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors
rows: Hyperglycemia, necrolytic migratory erythema, weight loss
Inhibition of insulin, CCK, enzymes, gastrin
Multiple or distal peptic ulcers, diarrhea
Parietal cell hyperplasia and acid hypersecretion
cAMP-driven intestinal chloride and water secretion
blocks.caption: Each syndrome is the normal action of one islet or gut hormone, amplified and unregulated.

blocks.text: Parathyroid chief cells release PTH according to the extracellular Ca2+ concentration sensed by the calcium-sensing receptor. Normally, a rise in serum calcium above the reference range (about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL, or 2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L) suppresses PTH. Primary hyperparathyroidism occurs when parathyroid tissue becomes less responsive to calcium, and its three pathologic forms differ in how many glands are involved and whether the tissue is clonal.

An adenoma causes about 85 percent of primary hyperparathyroidism. It is a single enlarged, encapsulated gland made mostly of chief cells, with little of the stromal fat that normal glands contain, and a rim of compressed normal parathyroid is often seen at its edge. The adenoma is a clonal growth, often with cyclin D1 overexpression or a somatic MEN1 mutation, whose calcium set point is shifted upward, so it keeps secreting PTH despite hypercalcemia. The high calcium in turn suppresses the other three glands, which are normal or small. This is why localization imaging shows a single focus.

Primary hyperplasia accounts for most of the rest. All four glands enlarge, although often unequally, and chief cells predominate. It may be sporadic but is the typical pattern in MEN1 and MEN2A, where every parathyroid cell carries the germline mutation. Multigland disease explains why hyperparathyroidism in MEN syndromes tends to recur.

Parathyroid carcinoma is rare, under about 1 percent of cases. It produces very high calcium (often above 14 mg/dL, or 3.5 mmol/L) and very high PTH, sometimes with a palpable, firm neck mass. Cytology cannot reliably separate it from adenoma, so the diagnosis rests on invasion of surrounding tissue or metastasis. Germline or somatic CDC73 mutations, encoding parafibromin, are associated.

blocks.title: Three forms of primary hyperparathyroidism
blocks.caption: Gland number and evidence of invasion separate the three; the hormone pattern of high calcium with high or inappropriately normal PTH is shared.

blocks.text: Pituitary adenomas are benign monoclonal tumors of anterior pituitary cells. They are classified in two ways. By size, a microadenoma is under 1 cm and a macroadenoma is 1 cm or larger; size matters because macroadenomas cause mass effects (C08). By function, an adenoma either secretes a hormone in excess or is clinically nonfunctioning, and immunostaining identifies the cell lineage either way. Many nonfunctioning adenomas are gonadotroph adenomas that make little or no biologically active hormone. Some adenomas arise in MEN1 (C15), and somatotroph adenomas often carry activating GNAS mutations that keep cAMP signaling on.

blocks.title: Pituitary adenomas by cell type
rows: Galactorrhea, hypogonadism; most common functioning type
Gigantism before epiphyseal closure, acromegaly after (EN-12-A)
blocks.caption: Hormone excess defines the functioning adenomas; gonadotroph adenomas usually present by size alone.

blocks.text: The prolactinoma is the most common hormone-secreting pituitary adenoma. Prolactin is the only anterior pituitary hormone under predominantly inhibitory hypothalamic control: dopamine from the arcuate nucleus reaches lactotrophs through the portal vessels and acts on D2 receptors to suppress prolactin synthesis and release. A prolactinoma escapes this control, and serum prolactin roughly parallels tumor size; values above about 200 ng/mL (normal is roughly under 20 to 25 ng/mL) are characteristic of a macroprolactinoma.

Most effects of prolactin excess come from suppression of GnRH. High prolactin inhibits the hypothalamic neurons that drive GnRH pulses, so LH and FSH fall. In women this causes anovulation, oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, and infertility, while prolactin acting on estrogen-primed breast tissue causes galactorrhea. In men, low LH lowers testosterone, causing decreased libido, erectile dysfunction, and sometimes gynecomastia; galactorrhea is uncommon because the male breast lacks estrogen priming. In both sexes, the resulting low sex steroid levels cause bone loss. Because menstrual change is noticed early, women usually present with microadenomas, whereas men often present later with macroadenomas and headache or visual loss.

A raised prolactin is not always a prolactinoma. Pregnancy, dopamine antagonist drugs, primary hypothyroidism (TRH stimulates lactotrophs), chronic kidney disease (reduced clearance), and stalk compression all raise it, and each has a mechanistic explanation.

sections.title: Mass effects of a nonfunctioning macroadenoma

blocks.text: The pituitary sits in the sella turcica, roofed by the diaphragma sellae. The optic chiasm lies just above, the cavernous sinuses (containing the internal carotid artery and cranial nerves III, IV, V1, V2, and VI) lie on each side, and the sphenoid sinus lies below. A nonfunctioning macroadenoma secretes nothing to draw attention, so it grows silently until it presses on these neighbors or on the normal gland.

Upward growth reaches the chiasm. In the chiasm, fibers from the nasal half of each retina cross, and these fibers carry the temporal visual fields. Midline compression therefore causes bitemporal hemianopia. Because a pituitary tumor pushes up from below, the inferior crossing fibers, which serve the superior temporal fields, are usually affected first, producing a superior bitemporal quadrantanopia early. Headache comes from stretching of the dura and diaphragma sellae. Lateral extension into the cavernous sinus can cause diplopia and ptosis, most often from cranial nerve III involvement.

Compression of the normal anterior pituitary and its portal blood supply causes hypopituitarism. Loss typically follows the order GH first, then LH and FSH, then TSH, with ACTH usually last, so early signs are subtle (hypogonadism, fatigue) and adrenal insufficiency appears late. Diabetes insipidus is uncommon with adenomas, because ADH is made in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior lobe, which are rarely injured by slow anterior growth; its presence suggests craniopharyngioma or another hypothalamic lesion.

Prolactin is the one hormone that rises. Compression of the stalk blocks dopamine delivery to normal lactotrophs, releasing them from inhibition (the stalk effect). The rise is mild, usually below about 100 ng/mL. Sudden hemorrhage or infarction of an adenoma (pituitary apoplexy) causes abrupt severe headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia, and acute ACTH deficiency.

blocks.title: Worked example: prolactinoma or stalk effect?
blocks.text: A 52-year-old man has headaches and bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 3 cm sellar mass. Prolactin is 60 ng/mL, and morning cortisol and testosterone are low. A prolactinoma this large would usually produce prolactin in the hundreds or thousands of ng/mL, because secretion tracks tumor mass. A mild rise with a large tumor means the stalk is compressed and normal lactotrophs have lost dopamine inhibition. Low cortisol and testosterone reflect compression of the remaining gland. This is a nonfunctioning macroadenoma, not a prolactinoma.

Rathke pouch is an upgrowth of oral ectoderm from the roof of the primitive mouth that forms the anterior pituitary. Normally its stalk regresses, but nests of squamous epithelium can persist along the path from the pharynx to the sella. A craniopharyngioma is a benign epithelial tumor arising from these remnants, usually in the suprasellar region above the pituitary. It is the most common tumor of the sellar region in children, and it has a bimodal age distribution, with a peak in childhood and a second peak in middle and older adulthood.

The childhood form, the adamantinomatous type, is the classic exam picture. It is partly solid and partly cystic, and the cysts contain thick, brownish, cholesterol-rich fluid often compared to machinery oil. It frequently calcifies, so a calcified suprasellar mass in a child on imaging strongly suggests this tumor. Histology shows stratified squamous epithelium with palisading basal cells, stellate reticulum, and nodules of wet keratin. These tumors carry activating mutations of CTNNB1 (beta-catenin). The adult papillary type is usually solid, rarely calcifies, and carries BRAF V600E mutations.

Although histologically benign, craniopharyngiomas adhere to and compress vital structures, and their effects follow from location. Pressing on the chiasm from above causes bitemporal hemianopia, often starting in the inferior temporal fields because the superior crossing fibers are reached first. Involvement of the hypothalamus and stalk injures the supraoptic and paraventricular neurons or their axons, causing central diabetes insipidus with polyuria and polydipsia. Loss of GHRH and GH, along with other pituitary hormones, causes growth failure and delayed puberty in children. Obstruction of the third ventricle can cause hydrocephalus, adding to headache and vomiting, and hypothalamic damage can cause obesity and sleep or temperature disturbance.

blocks.title: Craniopharyngioma compared with pituitary adenoma
blocks.caption: Calcification, diabetes insipidus, and young age point to craniopharyngioma rather than adenoma.

blocks.text: A follicular adenoma is a benign, solitary, encapsulated tumor of thyroid follicular cells. It forms uniform follicles that differ in pattern from the surrounding gland, which it compresses. Most adenomas are nonfunctional and appear cold on radioiodine scan; a minority carry activating mutations of the TSH receptor or Gs signaling pathway, become autonomous, and appear hot (toxic adenoma).

Follicular carcinoma is the second most common thyroid cancer, about 5 to 15 percent of cases, more frequent in women in middle age and in iodine-deficient regions. RAS mutations and the PAX8-PPARG fusion are typical. Its cells look the same as those of an adenoma: uniform follicular cells forming small follicles, without the nuclear features of papillary carcinoma. Malignancy is defined not by cell appearance but by behavior in tissue: penetration through the full thickness of the capsule or invasion of blood vessels within or beyond the capsule.

This explains a classic limitation. Fine needle aspiration samples individual cells, and identical cells cannot reveal capsular or vascular invasion, so cytology reports only a follicular neoplasm. The distinction requires excision and examination of the entire capsule. Minimally invasive tumors have an excellent prognosis, while widely invasive tumors behave more aggressively.

Because follicular carcinoma invades veins rather than lymphatics, it spreads hematogenously, most often to bone (lytic lesions, sometimes the first sign) and lung, and less often to brain and liver. Regional lymph node involvement is uncommon, which contrasts with papillary carcinoma. Well-differentiated metastases may still trap iodine and make thyroglobulin, reflecting retained follicular cell function.

blocks.title: Separating follicular adenoma from carcinoma
steps: Thyroid nodule aspirated
Cytology: uniform follicular cells, 'follicular neoplasm'
Nodule excised and entire capsule examined
No capsular or vascular invasion: follicular adenoma
Capsular penetration or vascular invasion: follicular carcinoma
blocks.caption: Invasion is a tissue architecture finding, so the diagnosis is made on the excised nodule, not on cytology.

blocks.text: Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, about 80 to 85 percent of cases. It arises from follicular cells, occurs most often in women between about 25 and 50 years of age, and usually presents as a painless, cold nodule or as an enlarged cervical lymph node. The best established environmental risk factor is ionizing radiation to the neck, particularly in childhood, as seen after the Chernobyl accident and after childhood head and neck radiotherapy.

Two genetic routes activate the same MAP kinase signaling pathway. The BRAF V600E point mutation is the most common alteration in sporadic tumors. RET/PTC rearrangements, which fuse the RET tyrosine kinase domain to the promoter and amino-terminal portion of a constitutively expressed gene, are particularly frequent in radiation-associated tumors, because radiation causes double-strand DNA breaks that can rejoin into fusion genes.

The diagnosis rests on nuclear features rather than invasion, which is why aspiration cytology works well here. The nuclei have finely dispersed chromatin that looks optically clear or empty, called ground glass or Orphan Annie eye nuclei. Folds in the nuclear membrane appear as longitudinal nuclear grooves, and invaginations of cytoplasm into the nucleus appear as intranuclear pseudoinclusions. Many tumors form branching papillae with fibrovascular cores. Psammoma bodies, concentric laminated calcifications, are thought to form when the tips of papillae infarct and undergo dystrophic calcification. Some tumors grow in a follicular pattern but are still papillary carcinomas because they have these nuclei.

Papillary carcinoma spreads through lymphatics, and spread to cervical lymph nodes is common, sometimes before the primary is palpable. Even so, prognosis is excellent, with 10-year survival above 90 percent, and nodal disease has little effect on survival in younger patients. Older age, large size, and spread beyond the thyroid worsen the outlook.

blocks.title: Papillary versus follicular carcinoma
blocks.caption: Nuclei define papillary carcinoma; invasion defines follicular carcinoma, and their spread differs accordingly.

blocks.text: Medullary carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor of the parafollicular C cells, which sit between follicles, concentrated in the upper and middle thirds of the lateral lobes, and secrete calcitonin. It accounts for about 5 percent of thyroid cancers. Because it does not arise from follicular cells, it does not make thyroid hormone or thyroglobulin and does not trap iodine.

Calcitonin is the tumor's signature. Serum calcitonin is raised and is used as a tumor marker. Calcitonin lowers calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, but in adult humans the effect is weak and overridden by PTH, so hypocalcemia is rare even when calcitonin is very high. Many tumors also secrete carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA), and some secrete other peptides, causing diarrhea or occasionally ectopic ACTH and Cushing syndrome.

Histologically, polygonal or spindle cells form nests and sheets within an amyloid stroma. The amyloid is derived from calcitonin precursor molecules that fold into beta-pleated sheets, and like all amyloid it stains with Congo red and shows apple-green birefringence under polarized light. Immunostaining for calcitonin, chromogranin, and CEA confirms the cell type.

About 70 to 80 percent of cases are sporadic and usually present as a single nodule in older adults. The rest are inherited through germline gain-of-function mutations of RET, a proto-oncogene on chromosome 10 encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase; constant RET signaling drives C cell proliferation. Inherited forms occur in MEN2A, MEN2B, and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma. They present earlier, are often bilateral and multicentric, and arise from a precursor stage of C cell hyperplasia, because every C cell carries the mutation. In MEN2 the penetrance of medullary carcinoma approaches 100 percent. Medullary carcinoma spreads to cervical nodes and through blood to liver, lung, and bone.

blocks.title: Sporadic and hereditary medullary carcinoma
blocks.caption: A germline mutation in every C cell produces multiple, earlier tumors.

sections.title: Euthyroid goiter and the thyroid nodule

blocks.text: A goiter is any enlargement of the thyroid. A nontoxic (euthyroid) goiter is enlargement without hyperthyroidism and, by the time it is recognized, without hypothyroidism. It forms through compensation: when hormone synthesis is impaired by iodine deficiency, dietary goitrogens, or a partial inherited defect of hormone synthesis, a small rise in TSH stimulates follicular cell hypertrophy and hyperplasia. The enlarged gland makes enough hormone, so TSH returns to the normal range while the gland stays big.

Early on the enlargement is diffuse (simple goiter), with hyperplastic follicles and later colloid-filled follicles as the stimulus waxes and wanes. With repeated cycles of hyperplasia and involution, the gland becomes multinodular. Follicular cells differ in their growth response, so some clones expand into nodules, and hemorrhage, fibrosis, calcification, and cysts follow. Multinodular goiters can become very large and extend behind the sternum. Their effects are mechanical: tracheal compression causes dyspnea and stridor, esophageal compression causes dysphagia, and venous obstruction at the thoracic inlet causes facial congestion. Nodules that become autonomous convert the gland to toxic multinodular goiter (EN-12-A).

The challenge is distinguishing a nodular goiter from a neoplasm. Thyroid nodules are common, and only a small minority, about 5 percent in most series, are malignant. Features that raise concern include a solitary nodule, male sex, very young or older age, a history of neck radiation, a hard or fixed nodule, rapid growth, hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve invasion, and enlarged cervical nodes. A goiter with several soft nodules, slow growth, and normal TSH favors a benign process.

Radioiodine scintigraphy shows whether a nodule traps iodide. A hot nodule takes up more iodine than the surrounding gland, reflecting autonomous function, and is almost never malignant. A cold nodule takes up less, which is expected of tissue that has lost differentiated follicular functions such as sodium-iodide symporter expression; this includes most carcinomas. Cold nodules therefore carry a higher cancer risk, about 10 percent, although most are still benign cysts, colloid nodules, or adenomas.

blocks.title: Euthyroid goiter versus thyroid neoplasm
blocks.caption: Normal TSH does not exclude cancer; nodule pattern, growth, and local invasion carry the weight.

blocks.text: Anaplastic (undifferentiated) carcinoma is the least common but most lethal thyroid cancer, under about 5 percent of cases. It occurs mainly in older adults, with a mean age around 65 years. Many arise from a preexisting well-differentiated papillary or follicular carcinoma or occur in a long-standing goiter, and the tumor shares the precursor's BRAF or RAS mutation.

Progression to anaplastic carcinoma is driven by inactivating mutations of TP53, which encodes the p53 tumor suppressor. Loss of p53 removes the cell cycle arrest and apoptosis that normally follow DNA damage, so genomic instability accelerates and the cells lose their follicular identity. The tumor no longer traps iodine, makes little or no thyroglobulin, and often loses thyroid transcription factor expression. Histologically it is composed of highly pleomorphic giant cells, spindle cells resembling a sarcoma, or both, with many mitoses and necrosis.

The clinical picture follows from very rapid growth and local invasion. A bulky neck mass enlarges over weeks and invades the trachea, esophagus, recurrent laryngeal nerve, and great vessels, causing dyspnea, stridor, dysphagia, and hoarseness. Distant metastases to lung are common at presentation. Prognosis is very poor, with median survival measured in months and death usually from local airway invasion. A sudden, rapidly enlarging mass in an older patient with a long-standing goiter or a treated differentiated cancer is the classic setting.

blocks.title: Thyroid carcinomas side by side
blocks.caption: Differentiation falls and aggressiveness rises from papillary to anaplastic; medullary stands apart by cell of origin.

blocks.text: The multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) syndromes are autosomal dominant disorders in which a germline mutation predisposes several endocrine glands to hyperplasia and tumors. They tend to present younger than sporadic tumors, involve multiple glands or multiple tumors within a gland, and recur. The two main types arise by opposite genetic mechanisms.

MEN1 is caused by an inactivating mutation of MEN1 on chromosome 11, which encodes menin, a nuclear tumor suppressor that restrains proliferation. One defective copy is inherited in every cell; a tumor forms when the second copy is lost in a particular cell, following the two-hit hypothesis. Primary hyperparathyroidism from multigland hyperplasia is the most common and usually first feature. Pancreatic and duodenal neuroendocrine tumors follow, most often gastrinomas (frequently small, multiple, and in the duodenum, causing Zollinger-Ellison syndrome) and insulinomas. Pituitary adenomas, most often prolactinomas, complete the classic triad. Hypercalcemia raises gastrin and acid secretion, which can worsen ulcer disease in these patients.

MEN2A and MEN2B are caused by gain-of-function mutations of the RET proto-oncogene on chromosome 10, encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase that is constitutively active. One mutant allele is enough, so penetrance is high, and the tissues affected are those that express RET, notably C cells and chromaffin cells. Medullary thyroid carcinoma occurs in nearly all carriers of both types, and pheochromocytoma occurs in about half. MEN2A adds parathyroid hyperplasia. MEN2B, from a different RET mutation (most often M918T), lacks hyperparathyroidism but adds mucosal neuromas of the lips and tongue, intestinal ganglioneuromatosis, and a marfanoid habitus; its medullary carcinoma begins in early childhood and is the most aggressive.

blocks.title: MEN syndromes
blocks.caption: MEN1 targets parathyroid, pancreas, and pituitary; both MEN2 types target C cells and chromaffin cells, and only MEN2A adds the parathyroid.

blocks.text: A pheochromocytoma is a tumor of chromaffin cells of the adrenal medulla that synthesizes and secretes catecholamines; identical tumors outside the adrenal, in sympathetic paraganglia, are called paragangliomas. The medulla is the only major site with abundant phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PNMT), which converts norepinephrine to epinephrine and is induced by the high cortisol draining from the cortex. Adrenal tumors therefore often make epinephrine, whereas extra-adrenal tumors mostly make norepinephrine.

Release may be episodic, continuous, or both, and the manifestations are those of adrenergic receptor stimulation. Alpha-1 vasoconstriction raises blood pressure and causes pallor; beta-1 stimulation causes tachycardia, palpitations, and forceful contraction. The classic triad is episodic headache, sweating, and palpitations with paroxysmal or sustained hypertension. Catecholamines also raise glucose (glycogenolysis plus alpha-2 inhibition of insulin) and metabolic rate, causing weight loss and anxiety. Chronic vasoconstriction contracts plasma volume, so orthostatic hypotension can coexist with hypertension. Spells can be triggered by pressure on the tumor, exertion, or anesthesia, and prolonged catecholamine excess can injure the myocardium.

Diagnosis exploits catecholamine metabolism. Tumor cells contain catechol-O-methyltransferase (COMT), which continuously converts norepinephrine and epinephrine to normetanephrine and metanephrine and releases them independently of the episodic catecholamine bursts. Plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine fractionated metanephrines are therefore raised even between spells and are more sensitive than catecholamines or VMA. Histologically the cells form nests (Zellballen) surrounded by sustentacular cells and stain for chromogranin. No histologic feature reliably predicts behavior; malignancy is defined by metastasis.

A substantial fraction, now estimated at about 30 to 40 percent, is hereditary, so bilateral tumors or young age suggest a syndrome. Associations include MEN2A and MEN2B (RET), von Hippel-Lindau disease (VHL, with hemangioblastomas and renal cell carcinoma), neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1, with neurofibromas and cafe-au-lait macules), and succinate dehydrogenase (SDH) mutations, which favor paragangliomas.

blocks.text: An endocrine paraneoplastic syndrome occurs when a tumor of a nonendocrine organ secretes a hormone or hormone-like peptide, and it is not subject to normal feedback. Because the source is outside the normal axis, the hallmark is a high hormone effect with the physiologic regulator of that effect suppressed. These syndromes can appear before the cancer is found.

Small cell lung carcinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor, and its cells can produce peptide hormones. Ectopic ACTH causes Cushing syndrome that often develops rapidly; cortisol levels may be so high that weight loss, muscle weakness, hypokalemia from cortisol action at mineralocorticoid receptors, and hyperpigmentation from very high ACTH dominate, rather than the slowly developing typical habitus. ACTH and cortisol are both high and do not suppress with high-dose dexamethasone, unlike a pituitary corticotroph adenoma (EN-12-A). Ectopic ADH causes SIADH: water is retained, producing euvolemic hyponatremia with inappropriately concentrated urine and continued urinary sodium loss (EN-12-A).

Hypercalcemia is the most common paraneoplastic syndrome overall. In the humoral form, the tumor secretes PTH-related peptide (PTHrP), whose amino-terminal region resembles PTH closely enough to activate the PTH1 receptor. It therefore increases osteoclastic bone resorption, increases renal calcium reabsorption, and causes phosphaturia. The rising calcium acts on the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor and suppresses native PTH. PTHrP is a weak stimulus for renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase, so calcitriol is usually not raised, unlike primary hyperparathyroidism. Classic sources are squamous cell carcinomas (lung, head and neck, esophagus), renal cell carcinoma, and breast carcinoma. Hypercalcemia from cancer can also arise from osteolytic bone metastases (breast, multiple myeloma) and from calcitriol made by some lymphomas; PTH is suppressed in all of these.

integration.text: Embryology and anatomy explain much of this chapter. Neural crest derived cells of the adrenal medulla give rise to neuroblastoma and pheochromocytoma, which share catecholamine chemistry but differ in age and maturity, and Rathke pouch remnants explain why craniopharyngioma sits above the sella and calcifies. The position of the optic chiasm, cavernous sinus, and hypothalamus predicts the mass effects of sellar tumors. Within the thyroid, the follicular cell gives papillary, follicular, and anaplastic carcinoma, while the C cell gives medullary carcinoma, which is why only medullary carcinoma makes calcitonin and is tied to MEN2.

Physiology and genetics explain the laboratory patterns. Autonomous secretion with suppressed regulators recurs throughout: high insulin with high C-peptide in insulinoma, atrophic remaining glands beside a cortisol adenoma or parathyroid adenoma, and suppressed PTH in hypercalcemia of malignancy. MEN1 illustrates tumor suppressor loss and MEN2 illustrates proto-oncogene activation, while TP53 loss drives anaplastic transformation. Limits apply: percentages vary between series, histology cannot always predict behavior (follicular lesions, pheochromocytoma), and a single test value must be read with the clinical setting.

summary: Adrenal cortical adenomas are small, lipid rich, and usually nonfunctional; carcinomas are large, invasive, and often virilizing; metastases outnumber primary carcinoma.
Neuroblastoma is a childhood neural crest tumor with Homer Wright rosettes, high urine HVA and VMA, MYCN amplification marking aggressive disease, and paraneoplastic opsoclonus-myoclonus.
Insulinoma secretes insulin despite low glucose, giving high insulin, C-peptide, and proinsulin with low ketones; exogenous insulin gives high insulin with low C-peptide.
Liver failure, sepsis, adrenal insufficiency, and alcohol cause hypoglycemia with appropriately low insulin.
Glucagonoma causes hyperglycemia, necrolytic migratory erythema, and weight loss; somatostatinoma causes diabetes, gallstones, steatorrhea, and achlorhydria by broad inhibition.
Parathyroid adenoma is one gland with the others suppressed; hyperplasia involves all four, as in MEN1 and MEN2A; carcinoma shows very high calcium and invasion.
Prolactinoma suppresses GnRH, causing amenorrhea, infertility, and galactorrhea in women and low libido in men; a large mass with mild hyperprolactinemia suggests stalk effect.
Macroadenomas cause bitemporal hemianopia, headache, and hypopituitarism; craniopharyngioma is a calcified suprasellar Rathke pouch tumor causing diabetes insipidus and growth failure.
Papillary carcinoma is diagnosed by nuclei and spreads by lymphatics; follicular carcinoma is diagnosed by invasion and spreads by blood; anaplastic carcinoma is TP53 driven and rapidly fatal.
Medullary carcinoma comes from C cells, makes calcitonin and amyloid, and is tied to RET and MEN2; pheochromocytoma is diagnosed by metanephrines, and PTHrP hypercalcemia has suppressed PTH.

verify: Percentages vary between sources: neuroblastoma arising in the adrenal (about 40%), MYCN amplification (about 20 to 25%), parathyroid adenoma (80 to 85%), papillary (80 to 85%), follicular (5 to 15%), medullary (about 5%), anaplastic (under 5%), and hereditary pheochromocytoma (about 30 to 40%, replacing the older rule of 10s).

Adrenal size cutoffs (adenoma usually under about 4 cm; carcinoma often over 6 cm) and the unenhanced CT threshold of about 10 Hounsfield units follow common imaging guidance; confirm the values NABNE expects.

The 72-hour fast criteria for endogenous hyperinsulinism (glucose under 55 mg/dL with insulin at least 3 microunits/mL, C-peptide at least 0.6 ng/mL, proinsulin at least 5 pmol/L, and suppressed beta-hydroxybutyrate) are from Endocrine Society guidance and were not stated in the text; confirm if NABNE tests the numbers.
The proportion of insulinomas in MEN1 (about 5 to 10%) varies between sources.
Prolactin thresholds (over about 200 ng/mL for macroprolactinoma; stalk effect usually under about 100 ng/mL, with some sources using up to 150 or 200 ng/mL) differ among references and assays.
The share of cold nodules that are malignant is quoted from about 5% to 20%; this chapter uses about 10%.

Some reviews list prolactinoma as the most common pituitary adenoma overall, while surgical series find nonfunctioning (gonadotroph) adenomas about as common; the text states the consensus that it is the most common hormone-secreting type.

The C cell origin of medullary carcinoma is traditionally given as neural crest, but lineage studies suggest an endodermal origin; the text avoids stating either and NABNE expectations should be confirmed.
MEN2B is reclassified as MEN3 in some recent classifications, and MEN4 (CDKN1B) is not covered; confirm the nomenclature NABNE uses.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Whipple triad, Homer Wright rosettes, Orphan Annie eye nuclei, Zellballen, and Zollinger-Ellison, or only the descriptive terms.
